fields.title: Where Product Logic Lives
fields.keyTakeaway: A rule on the server changes in minutes and cannot be bypassed, a rule on the client changes in weeks and is visible to everyone — therefore, placing a rule is a product decision about its flexibility.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: You ask to change the minimum order amount from 500 to 700 rubles. In one product this takes an hour, in another — three weeks. The difference is not the team.
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A PM who does not know where a rule lives cannot estimate either the change timeline or the risk. Worse, they do not participate in deciding where to place this rule during development, which is precisely when it is determined whether it will be flexible later. A rule that accidentally ends up on the client is frozen for years.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The minimal model: the [[client|client]] sends a [[request|request]], the [[server|server]] responds.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: The client is the program on the user's device: mobile app, browser website. The server is the program in the data center. There is a network between them, and each call costs time.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The key distinction for the product is not technical, but **the speed of change**:
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/rows/1/1: Days and weeks, some will never update
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Hence the placement rule: **everything that can change and everything that must not be bypassed lives on the server.** Minimum order amount, delivery cost, feature availability, promo conditions — on the server. Display and immediate reaction to actions remain on the client.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: A common mistake is rule duplication. The minimum amount check is done both on the client (to show the message immediately) and on the server (so it cannot be bypassed). This is normal and even correct, but it means two places to change. The correct form of duplication: the client does not store the number, but receives it from the server — then there remains only one rule.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The second consequence: **there are no secrets on the client.** Everything that ends up in the app can be extracted. A key hidden in code is not hidden.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: An audit of rules revealed three cases.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Minimum order amount* — on the server, comes in the cart response along with the message text. Changing the value is a config edit, works for everyone in a minute, including old app versions.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *List of available payment methods* — used to be on the client. When connecting a new payment method, it turned out that it would only appear for those who updated, i.e., about 60% in the first month. Moved to the server, spending a week on something that could have been avoided with the initial decision.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Delivery cost* — on the server, and that was non-negotiable: it depends on distance, time, and store; the client cannot calculate it even theoretically.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The rule the team established: **if the PM can imagine that a number might change someday, it comes from the server.**
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Not everything needs to go to the server. Phone format validation, cart total calculation for display, animations — on the client, otherwise the interface will become slow and unusable without a network. The boundary runs along the question "is it scary if the user bypasses this".
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A rule on the server changes in minutes and cannot be bypassed, a rule on the client changes in weeks and is visible to everyone — therefore, placing a rule is a product decision about its flexibility.
